title: EventChain: Consensus by Comparison
text:
Abstract
This paper defines EventChain, which records first and agrees afterwards. Whoever makes a reading, an estimate, an approval or a handoff signs it with their own key. Each signature covers everything before it, so nobody can change the past. One service, the Hub, orders and distributes the history as a file that every party with a stake in it keeps. At an agreed interval the Hub publishes one signed line that states the latest entry. Each holder verifies every entry by the same rules and compares its copy with that line, so every party knows that any other party checking against that line holds the same history through the entry it names, and reaches the same verdict on each entry. Agreement becomes a check each party runs for itself. A blockchain agrees first and records second, so every member must have built and paid for its system before the first entry is worth writing. In EventChain an entry costs one signature and one write, and one company can start without waiting for anyone else.
A valid chain shows which key signed what, and in what order. Whether a statement was true stays with its signer, and what to do about it stays with the application that acts on the evidence. Where strangers settle payments with one another, a blockchain’s round of votes remains the right tool.

title: 1  Executive Summary
text:
Value is moving onto digital claims, from tokenised property to electronic trade documents. A claim is only as sound as the checks behind it. In 2024 a video call faked every signal an employee of the engineering firm Arup relied on to know who was speaking. The employee transferred about US$26 million (Hong Kong Free Press 2024; CNN 2024). A company that cannot prove what happened carries the loss. The means to prove it already sit in people’s hands and in their machines. The FIDO Alliance reported five billion passkeys in use in May 2026 (FIDO Alliance 2026). Windows 11 requires hardware that can protect a signing key (Microsoft 2026). A forger who can fake a face and a voice cannot produce a signature from a key held in the signer’s own device (Section 2.2).
Suppose whoever made each reading, estimate, approval and handoff signed it with that key, as they made it. From that moment the history exists for everyone with a stake in it. The other side of the transaction holds it. So does the next owner, and the reviewer who arrives years later. An invoice arrives with its deliveries already agreed. A payment or an approval follows the evidence the moment it arrives, because the other side already holds it. The content behind each entry stays encrypted and readable only by those the parties allow. Software the parties allow can act on that content as soon as the evidence meets its rules, with no person checking each step again. Nothing waits for reconciliation. There is nothing left to reconstruct.
Many have tried to build that history on a blockchain. A blockchain agrees on each entry at the moment of writing, by a round of votes among its members. Every member must therefore have built and paid for its system before the first entry is worth writing, and every entry afterwards runs through that round. Four projects met that order in four ways. B3i, a consortium of insurers, closed in 2022. The chief executive of Swiss Re, a member, named the obstacle: it “would need all insurance companies to basically create smart contracts at the beginning” (Howard 2022). Everyone had to join before anything worked. With EventChain, one company starts recording on its own. The others take a copy when they need it. TradeLens connected ten ocean carriers. It still closed the same year. Rivals objected to putting their data on a platform that a competitor controlled (Hill 2018; United Nations ESCAP 2025). The agreement needs a place to happen, and at TradeLens that place belonged to a rival. With EventChain, each party checks its own copy. The service that distributes the history, the Hub, never sees what any document says. In 2022 ASX wrote off A$245–255 million. An independent review found little value in running all the business logic on a blockchain, because ASX already maintained the data’s integrity (Accenture 2022; ASX Limited 2022). Every entry waited for an agreement ASX did not need. In EventChain an entry costs one signature from whoever produced the event, and one write. The signature is the approval or the reading itself. Energinet designed its energy-certificate system to combine millions of fifteen-minute certificates into a single blockchain entry, citing the blockchain’s limited scalability and its cost (Energinet 2023). When every entry costs everyone’s agreement, readings come in bundles. In EventChain each reading is its own entry. EventChain exists to give the parties to a process the certainty a blockchain promises, that every one of them holds the same history, at the speed and cost of the work itself. It records first and agrees afterwards. Every holder compares its copy with one line that the Hub signs and publishes. This paper proposes that an independent foundation with no owners keep that line (Section 5.1). That comparison gives that certainty. This paper calls the result consensus by comparison (Chapter 3). The mechanism is in Chapter 4.
After those projects, recording every event looked unaffordable. Readings stayed bundled, and most events stayed out of any history. The art-registration service ascribe recorded on its farewell page that a marketplace weighing its service registered 100,000 photos a day, as many transactions as the whole Bitcoin network then handled, and that each photo needed its own provenance entry (ascribe team, n.d.). An entry that costs its maker’s signature and one write changes that. What becomes worth building is everything a blockchain made too expensive or too slow to record one event at a time; the worked examples take five such processes through. With every bill, an electricity supplier can send each fifteen-minute reading the meter’s key signed. The customer recomputes the total itself. An insurer and its policyholder can hold every estimate and revision behind a claim. A dispute then starts from evidence both already hold. An enterprise that hands confidential documents to an AI supplier can keep the supplier’s signed acknowledgment of each document version and the terms of its use. A lender can keep both valuations behind a mortgage approval. A later reviewer sees which one the approval relied on. A buyer of an aircraft part can check the signatures of the maker and each handler against registered keys before fitting it. Buyers once accepted forged paper certificates for such parts (Serious Fraud Office 2026).
A valid chain shows which key signed what, and in what order. The chain cannot show whether a statement was true. The party bound to the signing key answers for that (Section 3.3). The history records the approval or the transfer. Whatever moves the money or the title acts on that evidence, in the application or blockchain built for it (Section 3.5). The place to start is the process where waiting for reconciliation costs you most. The first entry is useful the day someone signs it. Nobody else has to agree first.

title: 2  Reconciliation After the Fact
text:
2.1 Histories Held in Slices
Suppose a buyer receives fewer cartons than the carrier’s invoice charges for. Each side reconstructs the delivery from its own records before comparing versions. Evidence can also control what happens before the goods leave. In the hypothetical dispatch application in Figure 2.1, a smart contract, software that enforces agreed conditions, checks signed commitments in EventChain. A missing acceptance holds dispatch; once the required evidence satisfies the rules, the dispatch system releases the shipment without another manual check.
Physical checks still establish whether the shipment matches the signed claims. The signed history remains intact while the handoff waits for acceptance. Applications can rely on that history only if it has five properties.
Organisations can verify objects better than histories. A certificate or a meter reading matters because of the actions around it: who issued it and who relied on it next. Those actions sit in emails and in each party’s own systems, so an outside party reconstructs the history when it needs one, from the parts it can reach.
Even two parties who trade every day lack a history of their shared work that both hold. In 2020, FreightWaves reported that up to 70% of Walmart Canada’s carrier freight invoices had “some sort of issue”, so staff spent their time sorting out the charges and carriers waited for payment, before the retailer and its carriers worked from one shared history of each shipment; afterwards, the carriers disputed fewer than 2% of more than 150,000 invoices (Tabak 2020). The invoices did not disagree because anyone lied. They disagreed because each side reconciled the shipment from its own records and met the other side’s version only at the invoice.
Where reconstruction falls short, organisations fill the gap with trust, as when a manufacturer trusts a supplier’s database. The supplier can change a record in it later, or show different parties different copies, and nobody outside would notice.

title: 2  Reconciliation After the Fact
text:
2.2 Why Now
Four changes make a history that outsiders can check worth more than it was five years ago: more value rests on digital claims, faking evidence has become cheap, the burden of proof is moving onto the company, and the tools to sign at source already sit in people’s hands.
Governments are moving transactions that once rested on paper onto digital claims. The UAE’s Digital Economy Strategy, launched in April 2022, “aims to double the contribution of the digital economy to the UAE’s gross domestic product (GDP) from 9.7 per cent in 2022 to 19.4 per cent within 10 years” (UAE Government 2022). Abu Dhabi has committed AED 13 billion over 2025–2027 to digitise and automate “100% of processes” in its government (Abu Dhabi Government Media Office 2025). Dubai Land Department forecasts that tokenised property will reach AED 60 billion, “7% of Dubai’s total real estate transactions”, by 2033; the figure is the department’s own forecast for a pilot launched in March 2025 (Dubai Land Department 2025). Trade documents are moving the same way. Under the UK’s Electronic Trade Documents Act 2023, “An electronic trade document has the same effect as an equivalent paper trade document” (s.3(2)) (UK Parliament 2023), and 13 jurisdictions have adopted UNCITRAL’s Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records, including Singapore and Abu Dhabi Global Market, several of them in part (United Nations Commission on International Trade Law 2025). A digital title or an electronic bill of lading is worth what the evidence behind it is worth: who checked the identity, who valued the asset, who approved the transfer, and in what order.
Faking the evidence has become cheap. In 2024 an employee in the Hong Kong office of the engineering firm Arup made 15 transfers totalling HK$200 million, about US$26 million, after a video call on which everyone except the employee was a deepfake (Hong Kong Free Press 2024; CNN 2024). The call carried every signal the employee normally relied on: familiar faces, familiar voices, a senior instruction. A check on who signed, with a key held in the signer’s own device, still holds, because a deepfake cannot produce that signature.
The burden of proof is moving onto the company. Since 21 June 2022, US Customs and Border Protection has presumed that forced labour made any goods produced wholly or in part in Xinjiang, and the importer must rebut the presumption (U.S. Customs and Border Protection 2026). The evidence that rebuts it originates with suppliers, their suppliers, and the facilities that made each input, each keeping its own records. An importer that cannot show that history in an order customs can check carries the loss.
The signing tools are already in place. The FIDO Alliance, the industry body behind passkeys, reported 5 billion passkeys in use worldwide in May 2026 (FIDO Alliance 2026), and Windows 11 requires “Trusted Platform Module (TPM) version 2.0” (Microsoft 2026). People already carry the credential that can sign a statement, and computers already hold hardware that can protect a signing key.

2.3 Who Keeps the History
Each generation of trust infrastructure changed whom an outside party has to trust, and only the last generation hands that party the whole history (Table 2.1).

Each earlier generation made the history easier to share, but each left the outsider holding a slice of it, which the outsider reconciles against other slices after the fact. In the last generation every interested party holds the whole history and reconciles it as it happens. The Hub, the one service that orders and distributes entries, publishes a signed statement of the newest entry at an agreed interval (a heartbeat). Each holder checks that every entry carries its producer’s signature over everything before it, and that its copy matches the latest heartbeat (Chapter 3).

2.3.1 Why Blockchains Stalled
Several enterprise blockchain consortia closed in 2022 and 2023. Their principals cited funding, participation, and commercial viability (A.P. Moller - Maersk 2022; Wragg 2022b, 2023a; McGee 2022). Participants named what consumed the money. One, quoted in Global Trade Review, called it “a business model problem more than anything … people underestimate the time and money required to reach critical mass” (Wragg 2022a). Swiss Re’s chief executive said of B3i, a consortium of insurers of which Swiss Re was a member: “It would need all insurance companies to basically create smart contracts at the beginning, at the origin” (Howard 2022). We read this as the architecture’s cost surfacing as a funding problem: a network that is useful only once most participants have joined needs financing until they do.
TradeLens reached ten ocean carriers and connectivity to about two-thirds of global containerised freight (IBM 2021), and still closed. In 2018, Hapag-Lloyd’s chief executive, Rolf Habben Jansen, named the objection: “each individual project claims to offer an industry platform that they themselves control. This is self-contradictory” (Hill 2018). The UN’s trade-digitalisation database records that “the shipping industry didn’t have the appetite for sharing confidential data with a competitor” (United Nations ESCAP 2025; Najati 2025). Price and the industry’s reliance on paper documents weighed as well; only 1.2% of bills of lading were electronic (PierNext 2023; Wragg 2023b). Neither cause belonged to the protocol, and both have moved since: electronic trade documents now carry the legal effect of paper (Section 2.2), and a history that costs one write per event has no per-container price to charge (Section 3.2).
Where one accountable operator already existed, a shared blockchain added little. ASX’s independent review found “little value to processing all the business logic on-ledger as ASX maintain data integrity as the market operator”, and that consensus contributed to round-trip latency; settlement runs of more than 100,000 transactions failed under load (Accenture 2022). ASX wrote off A$245–255 million (ASX Limited 2022).
The blockchain projects that lasted solved one business problem, treated the blockchain as an implementation detail, and had a party able to bring participants in: a regulatory mandate, a party with workflow authority, or an existing orchestrator (Gottlieb 2026). Where no such party exists, the last row of Table 2.1 needs no one to bring participants in, because each outside party checks the evidence it holds without joining anything.

title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
3.1 What You Get
The members of a ledger agree on the history before each append, by a round of votes among everyone present. The holders of an EventChain history agree after the append, each by comparing its copy with one line the Hub has signed and published (a heartbeat), and nobody has to be present. Both routes end in the same state: every party holds one history, and each knows that any other party checking against the same heartbeat finds the same history through the entry it covers. Because each holder applies the same rules to an identical copy, each reaches the same verdict on whether an entry follows them; only the payload check depends on what each holder may read (Section 4.7). That state is what consensus guarantees, and this paper uses the word for the guarantee. In the same way, a history with two or more holders is a distributed ledger in which the parties hold the copies and one Hub sets the order: many producers write, one Hub orders each topic, holders read, and no holder’s check depends on another holder.1 This chapter says “a ledger” for the kind that votes, and a history with one holder is a signed log. The two routes differ in when the agreement happens and who has to be present. The costs and limits of each route follow from that difference.
EventChain gives six of the eight guarantees people seek from a ledger without a round of votes, each under an assumption that Table 3.1 names, and leaves the other two to contract and to other layers.
The history is a text file that anyone can check with SHA-256 and ECDSA-P256, so the evidence outlives the platform that produced it.2 Every holder verifies every entry of its history, including entries whose payloads access policy keeps from it (Section 4.7). A gap in the chain or a copy shorter than the latest heartbeat shows that entries are missing, so a holder notices when a history leaves out inconvenient entries.3

title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
3.2 What It Costs
Because nobody has to be present at the append, an append is one write, and the work of recording grows with the number of events and with nothing else. Picture an electricity supplier with 10,000 meters, each signing a reading every fifteen minutes (worked example): 960,000 entries a day, about eleven a second. Whether the supplier can keep that history depends on whether the work grows with the number of events or with the number of parties who hold the history. On a ledger it grows with both.
In 2018, Hyperledger Fabric’s authors at IBM Research reported more than 3,500 transactions a second for a payment workload with five peers in one data centre, falling to between 1,400 and 2,000 with 100 peers across five data centres, every peer holding the whole ledger (Androulaki et al. 2018). The whole Ethereum network processed 3.6 million transactions on 28 April 2026, its busiest day up to October 2026 (Etherscan 2026); this one supplier’s readings would equal a quarter of that day. A consortium ledger recovers its costs from its users: in 2021, TradeLens listed its service from $8 per container (TradeLens 2021).
Suppose another logistics company joins a shipment process. Figure 3.1 follows the carrier’s signed acceptance: the company joins the consortium ledger as a validating member, or receives the EventChain history as a holder.

A ledger can also serve read-only users without adding validators, and consensus need not wait for every member’s vote. Adding an EventChain holder adds one copy of the file and that holder’s own checks; existing holders do not repeat verification for it. The application’s business rules still apply: if dispatch requires the new company’s acceptance, the smart contract waits for it (Figure 2.1).
The Hub checks each submitted line as a verifier does, for well-formedness, predecessor hash and signature, before it appends (Section 4.4). A benchmark of the reference Hub on 14 October 2026, on one thread per topic on an Apple M4 Max, committed more than 11,000 entries a second with all three checks on every line, and 29,000 with the head comparison alone, from one run (EventChain 2026a); the checks cost the Hub thread 65 microseconds a line (Section 4.5). No fee attaches to an event. Each holder receives one line of about 335 bytes per event and verifies its copy on its own processor at its own pace. A holder that verified yesterday’s copy checks only today’s new entries. These measurements describe different workloads and environments: observed Ethereum traffic is not network capacity, and the figures are not a comparative throughput benchmark.
Batching spreads the trip to the Hub across many events. A benchmark of the reference producer on 13 October 2026 measured it against a compare-and-append Hub model (EventChain 2026c). Each producer signed a sequence of entries, each over the one before, and submitted them together; the Hub accepted the whole batch when its first entry followed the current head, the predecessor-hash check that binds the batch to the whole history, and the benchmark then checked format and signatures on every output file: all 160 passed. title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
3.3 What Remains Trusted
Beyond the file and a verifier, a holder depends only on what the last column of Table 3.1 names, chiefly the enrolment evidence behind each key, the keeper of the heartbeat list and the Hub’s availability to accept new entries. The Hub cannot rewrite a signed entry. It can withhold entries from a holder or show different holders different histories; Figure 4.2 shows how a holder checks against the latest heartbeat. Two conflicting heartbeats under the Hub’s key attribute the fork to the Hub. The field calls these properties fork consistency and accountability (Section 4.4; adversarial Hub analysis). Deciding what to do with the evidence stays with the application. EventChain does not prevent a false entry at the moment of creation; it makes later denial and editing unattractive, because each entry names a signing key and binds its statement to the preceding history.4 Table 4 gives the boundary capability by capability.

title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
3.4 Where It Breaks
A valid signature proves that a key signed these bytes. It cannot reveal an honest mistake, coercion, collusion or a signer who signs without reading. Process controls and audit remain necessary, and when something goes wrong they now start from a signed history and the identity evidence behind it (failure-mode tables).

title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
3.5 When It Fits
EventChain fits where each party to a process answers for what it signs, and where at least one of them needs evidence that survives beyond any single platform. Because each party answers for what it signs, detection after the fact suffices. Because the evidence travels as a file, nobody has to join a network before the first entry is useful. Where strangers settle payments with one another, a ledger’s round of votes remains the right tool. Where one organisation controls the whole process and nobody outside needs to verify, an ordinary audit trail does. Table 9 sets each approach beside the others.

title: 3  Consensus by Comparison
text:
In the vocabulary of distributed systems, a topic is a single-writer replicated log (the Hub is the single appender; producers sign the entries it appends) with timeline consistency, the model of PNUTS, in which “all replicas of a given record apply all updates to the record in the same order” and a read returns a possibly stale version that “is always a valid one from the record’s history” (Cooper et al. 2008). Under PACELC (Abadi 2012), a topic chooses consistency over availability when partitioned, refusing to append against an unknown head or to act on evidence it cannot confirm, and latency over consistency otherwise, appending without waiting for holders; the heartbeat bounds undetected staleness to one publication interval while the heartbeat list stays reachable and preserves every heartbeat (Section 5.1). Abadi classifies PNUTS the same way, PC/EL.↩︎
Hash-linked time-stamping showed that ordering and tamper-evidence come from chained commitments with no round of votes (Haber and Stornetta 1991). Registry-style transparency architectures such as SCITT leave statement storage and distribution to implementers (Birkholz et al. 2026); the file and the Hub fill that gap. The standards comparison places them alongside earlier systems.↩︎
Parakeet frames a related pattern: public commitments, private querying and verifiable proof (Malvai et al. 2023).↩︎
Transparency systems hold issuers accountable after publication (Birkholz et al. 2026). The US Food and Drug Administration’s data-integrity guidance rejects shared logins for the same reason: “a unique individual cannot be identified through the login” (U.S. Food and Drug Administration 2018).↩︎

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.1 Append-Only File
Producers sign entries into an append-only file (AOF), a single Hub orders and distributes the file, and every holder verifies its own copy. A topic is one history (the events a deployment collects together in one AOF). Checking the chain and the producer signatures needs only the file and no trust in the Hub; naming the signer and confirming that a copy is current need further evidence (Section 4.9.1). The byte-level rules an implementer needs are in the Specification appendix.
The AOF is a JSON Lines (JSON Lines 2023) document, one JSON object per line. Each entry carries a salted hash of its payload, a locator for the payload, the SHA-256 hash of the previous line, the signer’s public key and an ECDSA-P256 signature over every other member (Table 4.1, Figure 4.1). Producers encrypt payloads before they reach the Hub, so the Hub holds or relays ciphertext only and never has plaintext or decryption keys.
Because the signature covers prev_hash, each producer signs its own position in the chain. Editing any line or moving an entry to a different predecessor invalidates a producer signature that the Hub cannot recreate, so the ordering guarantee rests on the producers’ keys. An entry’s unique identifier, its Event ID, is the SHA-256 hash of its exact written line, and later entries refer to earlier ones by it.

text:
4.2 Payload Hash
payload_hash is SHA-256(salt ‖ payload) over a fresh random salt followed by the exact plaintext bytes. Nobody without the salt can test guesses against the hash, and whoever holds the plaintext and the salt can recompute it, so each holder keeps the salt with the payload. The AOF names no signer, only a public key; the signer’s identity and role sit in the payload under access policy (Section 4.7).

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.3 What a Signature Proves
A device or a software service signs its entries directly: a sensor signs each measurement at source with a hardware-held key. A person’s passkey cannot sign arbitrary bytes, so the producing system signs the entry and the person confirms it in a separate Mint entry whose WebAuthn challenge is the confirmed entry’s Event ID (WebAuthn checks). In every case a valid signature proves that a key signed these bytes. What it proves about who acted depends on where the key lives (Table 4.2).



Table 4.2: What a valid signature proves for each kind of signer










Signer
Where the key lives
What a valid signature proves




Device
TPM, physically unclonable function (PUF) or secure element
This key signed these bytes. Binding the key to a particular device rests on enrolment or attestation evidence and on the key’s actual protection; the signature shows nothing about calibration, attachment or the measurement path

The passkey answered this challenge with the checked flags. Naming the person and role rests on enrolment evidence and passkey-control policy






A registry binds each public key to a person, device, service or role, with the enrolment evidence behind the binding. A registry is a topic like any other, and a holder verifies it with the same checks. It cannot write, reorder or block an entry in any other topic. A binding that others rely on carries two signatures, the subject’s offer and the registry keeper’s acceptance (registry conventions, three of them still open), so neither party creates it alone. An organisation keeps a registry for its own signers. An authority or community keeps one that binds each organisation’s root key to its legal identity. Each topic declares the registries it accepts, by root key directly or through a binding in a registry it already accepts. It changes that declaration only with its other parties’ countersignature, because otherwise the party that started the topic could swap registries and re-attribute past signatures. The chain of registries ends at a root key that the parties accept outside the protocol, as a browser accepts its root store (Reddy and Wallace 2010). A binding shows whom its keeper says a key belongs to.
A signature carries no ongoing authority and no time, so a departed employee’s earlier signatures stay valid. A lost key leaves the chain intact: the keeper retires it and the organisation enrols a new one. A compromised key differs, because someone else may sign with it. The keeper therefore signs a compromise claim that names the time from which the key is suspect, and the claim stands beside the history as a visible dispute that erases nothing. The verifier reports each entry the key signed between that time and the claim as inside the claimed window, and the application decides. The order between a registry entry and an entry in another topic is only as fine as the positions that the Hub’s signed heartbeats and the Bitcoin anchors cover (Section 4.4.1, Section 4.8), because no shared clock orders the two topics. The verifier reports signature validity, binding evidence, compromise status and authorisation separately.

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.4 Append Protocol
The head is the hash of the last line in the chain. A producer keeps the head it last appended or observed (its retained head) and submits against a verified expected head. Because the signature covers prev_hash, changing that field requires signing again.

The producer requests the current head and any entries since its retained head. It accepts a matching head with no new entries, or verifies an extension to the new head. If the Hub supplies a history that omits the retained head, the producer treats it as evidence of rollback or truncation and does not sign against it.
The producer sets prev_hash to the verified current head, signs the entry and submits it with that expected head.
The Hub accepts the entry only if its current head still matches the expected head. After the append, the producer retains the new head.
If another entry arrived first, the Hub rejects the submission. The producer obtains and verifies the new extension, updates prev_hash to the new head, signs the entry again and resubmits against that head.

The Hub applies to each submission exactly the checks a verifier applies to one line: the line is well formed under the entry specification, prev_hash equals the current head, and the key on the line signed it. It appends every submission that passes, whatever the entry says and whoever holds the key, and judges nothing else; a false statement or an unbound key enters the history, where the verifier reports it and the other parties contest it (Section 4.6). A submission that fails receives a signed refusal naming the submission hash, the reason and the Hub’s asserted time, which the submitter retains, so a refusal of a valid line is evidence against the Hub.
A valid chain can still be an old prefix, so the protocol requires the Hub to publish signed heartbeats to the heartbeat list. Every holder, including a first-time one, retrieves the latest heartbeat for its topic and checks its copy against it, and so detects an out-of-date copy or a diverging history without contacting other holders. Two conflicting heartbeats under the Hub’s key attribute the fork to the Hub. These are the established properties of fork consistency (Li et al. 2004) and accountability (Laurie et al. 2013). The publication interval bounds freshness, and the list must preserve every heartbeat and show everyone the same list.

4.4.1 Hub Heartbeat
A heartbeat carries the topic’s head, the entry count and the time of issue under the Hub’s signature. The Hub publishes one at the agreed interval even when no entries arrive. The keeper of the heartbeat list preserves every heartbeat for each topic and publishes the Hub key the topic accepts; Section 5.1 proposes who that keeper should be. Every holder compares its own copy with that common reference (Figure 4.2). The time is the Hub’s own assertion; independent timestamping can add external time evidence (Section 4.8). Heartbeat Encoding and Retrieval specifies the format and retrieval.
Suppose the Hub serves different histories to the buyer and warehouse in the dispatch application (Figure 2.1). Both copies pass their chain and producer-signature checks, but they contain different hashes at the same position. The warehouse detects the disagreement by comparing its hash with the common checkpoint (Figure 4.2), without contacting the buyer.

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.5 Scale and Ordering
The Hub appends on a single thread per topic, so each topic has one ordered history and different topics proceed independently. Each accepted entry costs one append and no multi-party consensus round. A holder that keeps a verified prefix verifies only the extension; Section 3.2 gives the measured rates.

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.6 Cryptographically Bound Contracts
A Cryptographically Bound Contract (CBC) records a two-party agreement as two entries: the offering party signs an offer, and the accepting party signs an acceptance that names the offer by its Event ID (CBC references). A custody transfer is one instance; a supplier’s acceptance of shared data under agreed terms is another (worked example). Until the acceptance exists the CBC is pending, and any party inspecting the chain sees the missing acceptance.
A correction, an objection or a resolution is likewise a new signed entry that names the entry it addresses (correction references). The original stays in the chain, no later statement overrides it automatically, and application policy decides who may make each kind of statement.

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.7 Access to Payloads
Applications decide which holders may retrieve and decrypt each payload, and a Hub or storage service can enforce that without holding decryption keys. A regulator may read every payload while a customer reads only those under its contract, yet both hold the same AOF and run the same checks on it (payload access and export). An application the parties authorise can act on the evidence as soon as it meets the application’s rules, with no person checking each step again.

title: 4  How EventChain Works
text:
4.8 OpenTimestamps
An optional daily OpenTimestamps (OTS) rollup anchors the current chain head in Bitcoin, which shows that the committed bytes existed before the time of a validated anchor (OpenTimestamps 2026; Todd 2016). That evidence relies on the Bitcoin network and on validation of the proof, independent of the Hub, and does not show when the events occurred. A Hub can anchor both branches of a fork, so OTS protects against neither split views nor stale copies.

text:
4.9 Verification
The verifier reports separate conclusions about a history (Table 4.3). A holder can check its chain and signatures without payload access, and can validate an external time proof without the plaintext. Hash links alone authenticate nothing; producer signatures authenticate the history.

title: 5  Open Protocol
text:
5.1 Protocol Stewardship
Holders can verify an EventChain history without access to the application that created it. They retain the file and use the verifier to check its chain and signatures, even after changing suppliers or closing an old system. Identity, payload, and time checks also need their supporting evidence (Section 4.9.1).
The file uses JSON Lines (JSON Lines 2023), SHA-256 and ECDSA-P256 (National Institute of Standards and Technology 2015, 2023), JCS (Rundgren et al. 2020) and WebAuthn (Hodges et al. 2021), so a verifier built from this paper confirms any AOF, past or present, whichever Hub produced it.
The public EventChain implementation repository contains the Haskell producer, a separate verifier package, and shared cryptography code under the BSD-3-Clause licence (EventChain 2026). The reference Hub lives in its own repository (EventChain Protocol 2026).
The holder’s checks are independent, each needing the evidence named in Table 4.3. Verification results inform an application decision; they do not authorise it.
Integration uses HTTP webhooks and REST endpoints. Subscribing systems (ERP platforms, evidence portals, consumer-facing applications, regulator dashboards) receive events as they occur and store their own verifiable copy. Application-level business logic determines which actions become evidence; holders receive the topic’s history, while application access policies govern payload retrieval and decryption.
Every check in this paper runs on one copy of the history. Each entry carries its producer’s signature, so the Hub cannot rewrite history. One power remains with the Hub: it can show one holder one history and another holder another, and each copy passes every check on its own.
The file alone already gives fork consistency: holders who compare copies with one another find the fork. That comparison is a distributed system, and EventChain exists so that no holder has to coordinate with another. A keeper of the heartbeat list strengthens the guarantee to the point where one holder, on its own, detects a fork or an old copy within one publication interval.
At each interval the Hub signs a heartbeat and publishes it to the heartbeat list (Section 4.4.1). Figure 4.2 shows how a holder compares its copy against that common reference, including a copy that ends early or diverges at the covered position. Two conflicting Hub-signed heartbeats for the same topic and position attribute a fork to the Hub; a mismatching copy alone does not. Publication is interval-based, so the current heartbeat covers the prefix up to its position, and entries after it await the next heartbeat.
The keeper of the heartbeat list needs little trust. It cannot forge a heartbeat, because the Hub signed it. It cannot read an entry, because a heartbeat carries only a hash, a count and a time. It can lie only by showing an old list, which a holder notices when no heartbeat arrives within the agreed interval, or by showing two holders two lists, which any two holders expose by setting their heartbeats side by side. Haber and Stornetta’s company printed its weekly hash as a classified advertisement in the New York Times for the same two properties: nobody can withdraw a printed line, and every reader sees the same page.
The heartbeat list is the one thing in the design that has to be neutral, so we propose that an independent foundation with no owners keep it, together with what every party already shares: the specification, the open-source verifier, the conformance suite, the identity-registry conventions and a signed list of recognised Hub service providers (the parties that run Hubs) for topics that span rivals. A founding authority convenes the foundation and controls neither its council nor its oversight; other authorities join that oversight as equals, and no supplier or founder decides alone.
A signature names a key. An entry is evidence only if someone stands behind that key and nobody can change later who that was. A registry settles the first: a topic, kept by any organisation or authority, in which the key owner and the registry keeper both sign each binding of a key to a person, device or role, so neither binds a key alone. The protocol settles the second: a registry cannot touch an entry in any other topic, and a topic changes which registries it accepts only when its other parties countersign, so nobody changes who signed a past entry by changing which registry answers. Every chain of registries ends at a root key that the parties accept outside the protocol, as a browser accepts its root store (Section 4.3). The foundation keeps the conventions those registries follow; binding a key stays the keeper’s act, and accepting a root stays the parties’. Who may keep a registry that others accept, and how a keeper recovers a lost root, are the first questions the foundation settles (registry conventions).

title: 5  Open Protocol
text:
5.2 Bootstrapping
One organisation starts on its own. It enrols the keys its people and devices already hold, runs a Hub for one process it already operates, and signs that process’s events into a topic. Its Hub publishes heartbeats from the first entry (Section 4.4.1). Each counterparty takes a copy of the file when it needs one, verifies it against the latest heartbeat, and so nobody waits for a consortium. The deployment tables list what a production deployment still has to put in place.

title: 6  Conclusion
text:
A process on EventChain leaves signed evidence of every reading, estimate, approval and handoff as it happens, and everyone with a stake in it holds the same history. Reconstruction after a shipment or a claim has no work left. A dispute opens from evidence both sides already hold.
Software can act on evidence it already holds. An approval that today waits for a person to check what the other side sent can follow the moment the evidence meets the rules the parties set, with the content still encrypted and readable only by those they allow (Section 4.7). That is what people hoped a blockchain’s programmable contracts would do. An audit becomes a read of a history instead of a reconstruction from both sides’ files. An asset carries its history to its next owner across companies and borders. The buyer checks it before paying. A tokenised title or an electronic bill of lading rests on evidence any recipient can check (Section 2.2). A regulator holds the history itself, with no report standing between. Every process in which you wait for someone else to confirm what happened is a candidate, and the ideas a blockchain priced out of reach are the first to look at (the worked examples).
None of this waits for an industry to agree. The specification and the verifier are open. Any party can run a Hub for its own topics (Chapter 5). One company can start with one process, and the others take a copy when they need it. We propose an independent foundation with no owners to keep the one line every holder checks against (Section 5.1). The first history can begin this quarter, in one process, with the keys your people already carry.

title: Appendix: Worked Examples
text:
Every Reading Behind the Bill
According to the undated farewell page of the art-registration service ascribe, a marketplace weighing the service was processing 100,000 photos a day, as many transactions as the whole Bitcoin network handled at the time. The ascribe team could not merge those registrations into a single blockchain entry, because each photo needed what it called “clean provenance” (ascribe team, n.d.). Everything worth keeping can become an entry that another party checks, at one signature and one append each, at whatever volume the work produces (What It Costs). An idea set aside because a blockchain could not carry its volume is worth building.
Each entry can also leave the system that collected it. A party who arrives later, such as an auditor, checks the history with an open verifier (5  Open Protocol) and does not need the application that produced it. Because every step enters the history, it keeps details whose importance nobody saw at the time.
Every example below is a process whose parties reconcile after the fact today, and in each one the dispute or audit instead starts from a history every party already holds. The examples share one arrangement. Keys held by people, devices, and software sign the entries, and the file carries only a hash of each document (Payload Hash). Each party that may later need to prove something keeps the documents it has a right to hold and the enrolment evidence for each signing key (What Each Check Needs).
Suppose a commercial customer disputes one quarter of its electricity bill. Its supplier answers with the history of every fifteen-minute reading behind the total. Each reading carries a signature from a key associated with the meter, and the customer checks the disputed readings, without access to the supplier’s billing system. A supplier can send that history with every bill and make checkable measurements part of its service.
One blockchain design compressed that level of detail. Energinet, Denmark’s electricity transmission system operator, stated in 2023 that certifying energy at fifteen-minute intervals requires 35,040 certificates per meter per year. Its Project Origin design for energy certificates combined millions of such transactions into a single blockchain entry, citing the blockchain’s limited scalability and its operating cost (Energinet 2023). In EventChain, each reading stays its own signed entry in the history the customer holds.
The supplier’s signed report identifies the exact reading entries it used. With authorised access, the customer retains the measurement contents alongside the history. A later assessor can check those readings against their signed entries and the report, without asking the supplier to reconstruct the evidence.
That evidence lets the parties locate a disputed reading, but its signature does not establish that the measurement was correct. The parties examine the evidence that links the signing key to the meter. Calibration records and physical inspection help assess whether the meter measured correctly at the right point.1

title: Appendix: Worked Examples
text:
Every Estimate Behind a Claim
Picture a policyholder who disputes a car-repair settlement lower than the repairer’s estimate. The insurer and the policyholder hold the same history of the claim: the photographs the policyholder sent, the repairer’s first estimate, the revised estimate after inspection, the assessment that recommended the settlement, and the adjuster’s approval. Both sides see which estimate the recommendation used, so the dispute starts from the evidence. An insurer can build that history for every claim as the claim develops.2
The recommendation names the revised estimate it used, and the approval names that recommendation; entry order alone does not show which evidence a decision used. A later correction adds a signed entry and keeps the earlier decision’s basis in view.3
A reviewer investigating a discrepancy can trace it to the contribution that introduced it, and the signature on that contribution shows which key signed it, so the party bound to that key answers for it.

title: Appendix: Worked Examples
section: Every Document Handed to an AI Supplier
text:
Every Document Handed to an AI Supplier
Imagine an enterprise that sends confidential design documents to an AI supplier for an automated review. The contract lets the supplier analyse the documents for the enterprise, and forbids it to train shared models on them or to disclose them to other customers. On receipt, the supplier signs an acknowledgment of the exact document version and those terms, and the enterprise keeps it. An enterprise can collect that acknowledgment for every version and permission change, and keep the evidence of what each supplier accepted after the relationship ends.
The concern is common: in Cisco’s 2024 Data Privacy Benchmark Study, 68% of 2,600 privacy and security professionals cited disclosure to the public or to competitors as a concern about generative AI (Cisco 2024).
The acknowledgment completes a two-party agreement, which Cryptographically Bound Contracts calls a Cryptographically Bound Contract (CBC): the enterprise’s entry offers the documents under the terms, and the supplier’s signed entry accepts them. The enterprise’s own entry shows only what the enterprise sent; the supplier’s signature makes the receipt evidence of what the supplier accepted.4 Each acceptance references the exact offer, even if other entries fall between them in the history.
If another customer’s output later reproduces a distinctive confidential passage, the enterprise’s reviewer checks the retained documents against their hashes and compares the passage with that output and its full prompting context. Researchers extracted training data from the production language models they studied (Nasr et al. 2023). The contract’s dispute process decides whether the supplier breached it, and the enterprise brings the evidence it already holds: the supplier’s acknowledgment of the particular material and the restrictions it accepted.

title: Appendix: Worked Examples
text:
Every Check Behind a Mortgage
Consider a lender that approves a mortgage after the valuer revises the valuation, because a new search found a right of way across the land. Years later, at refinancing, a reviewer asks which valuation the approval relied on. The history answers: both valuations remain as signed entries, and the approval references the revised one. A buyer or lender can keep that evidence for every property decision as the work happens, including the checks and revisions that never appear in the final approval.
Four contributors build the evidence behind an approval like this one (Table 1).5

title: Appendix: Worked Examples
text:
Every Handoff of a Part
Between January 2019 and July 2023, the UK parts trader AOG Technics sold more than 60,000 aircraft engine parts with forged Authorised Release Certificates, the documents that guarantee airworthiness. Its director doctored genuine certificates, and customers received documents carrying the signatures of sales and quality managers who did not exist. The fraud left planes grounded in the UK and worldwide, with estimated losses of more than £39.3 million for airlines, and came to light after an airline asked the aircraft equipment manufacturer Safran to check the authenticity of one part (Serious Fraud Office 2026). If the maker or maintenance organisation signs each release and handoff of a part, and the buyer can link that key to the organisation through an accepted key registry (What a Signature Proves), the buyer can check the chain before fitting the part. A doctored certificate then fails the signature check, and a manager who does not exist has no key bound to them.
The same evidence serves any asset owner who inherits equipment: the inspection findings, corrections, and handoffs that people sign as routine work proceeds.
For a compressor, an inspector’s finding and the fabricator’s correction remain in the history together. As in the claim example, a later approval references the evidence it accepted without removing the earlier finding. The next owner inherits the history and authorised access to the supporting material, so an investigation after installation can trace which findings and approvals preceded the failure.
The parties to each custody transfer keep an offer and signed acceptance, as in the AI example. The pair shows what the parties accepted; it does not by itself prove physical delivery or equipment condition.
The Hub publishes a heartbeat for the file (Hub Heartbeat), so a new owner can check before the purchase closes that its copy is complete and current.
A digital product passport (a product record shared with parties such as repairers and recyclers) can present selected information from the same history, so a repairer can examine maintenance evidence or a recycler retrieve the material information it may see. The EU’s Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation provides for passport information shared under access rights that differ by product group (European Parliament and Council 2024). The passport application decides who may see what and whether it meets the applicable requirements; EventChain supplies the signed history beneath it, so later checks need not depend on the original passport portal.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
Entry Specification
This appendix holds the byte-level rules that 4  How EventChain Works relies on.
Lines and rejection. Each line ends in 0x0a, and a file that contains 0x0d anywhere counts as malformed. A verifier that finds a malformed line under any rule in this appendix rejects the whole AOF and reports the line.
Field encodings. Every member of the entry object is a JSON string. Binary members use base64url without padding (Josefsson 2006, sec. 5):
entry_id and payload_ref are opaque strings with no encoding requirement.
Event ID. The Event ID (Append-Only File) excludes the row’s terminating 0x0a. After writing the row, the Hub derives and returns the Event ID and may record it in a separate lookup index. An application keeps evidence(row key, Event ID, salt) beside its existing data. The Hub answers lookups, and a holder checks each answer against the Event ID and its own copy of the chain.
entry.data(). The signed message entry.data() is the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (Rundgren et al. 2020) serialisation of the entry object without its signature member. The removal applies to exactly the member named signature; the signature covers every other member the declared revision permits. Because RFC 8785 orders members by name, producers may write members in any order on the line. An unknown member or an unsupported revision makes the entry malformed. Authenticating which topic a history belongs to also requires an accepted binding between the topic and its first entry, and that convention remains open.
Chain bytes. prev_hash is the SHA-256 digest of the previous line exactly as written: every byte after the preceding line terminator (or the start of the file), up to and excluding the previous line’s own 0x0a. A verifier applies no canonicalisation, so reformatting a line into a form a JSON parser would read as equivalent changes its hash and breaks the next entry’s predecessor check. The final line has no successor; a retained head or a heartbeat at or beyond it binds its exact bytes.
Figure 1 separates the two byte paths; the rules above define them.
Genesis. The first entry carries a prev_hash of 32 zero bytes, encoded like any other hash, and a verifier rejects an AOF whose first entry carries any other value.
Duplicate members. An entry in which any member name appears more than once counts as malformed. Parsers resolve duplicate names differently, so relying on a parser’s default would let one line verify two ways.
Unicode. An escape that denotes an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate in a member name or value counts as malformed; a verifier never substitutes a replacement character.
Revisions and Mint entries. The string member v declares the revision. Without it, an entry has the six base members; "1" also admits the Mint members in Table 1, which record a person’s confirmation of an earlier entry by passkey (What a Signature Proves). A verifier compares revision labels as strings, never as numbers. A revision-1 entry without Mint members is an ordinary producer-signed entry.
A Mint entry declares v = "1" and carries all six Mint members beside the base members. Partial or misplaced Mint members, or an unknown kind, make the entry malformed. The target must be an earlier verified entry in the same chain.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
WebAuthn Assertion Checks
For a Mint entry, the verifier checks three things, following the WebAuthn assertion format (Hodges et al. 2021). client_data_json must be valid UTF-8 JSON of type webauthn.get whose challenge equals the encoded target_hash. authenticator_data must hold at least 37 bytes, with the user-presence flag set and consistent backup-state flags. assertion_sig must verify under attester_key over authenticator_data ‖ SHA-256(client_data_json). These checks leave the relying party’s origin and RP ID policy, user verification and signature counter to the application’s accepted authentication context.

text:
Heartbeat Encoding and Retrieval
Signed format. The Hub takes position and head_hash in Table 2 from the same chain state.



Table 2: Heartbeat fields









Member
Meaning




v, kind
Literal values "1" and "heartbeat"


topic_id
Exact topic identifier from the agreed settings

Number of entries in the committed prefix, at least one


head_hash
SHA-256 of the exact final row in that prefix, excluding its terminating 0x0a

Hub-asserted issuance time, Unix seconds with an optional fractional part

The encoding is a UTF-8 JSON object with string values. The Hub signs the JCS serialisation of the other members and then adds signature, using ECDSA-P256 and the binary encodings of the entry specification. A verifier rejects duplicate or unknown members, unknown revisions, unpaired surrogates and malformed values. position uses ASCII decimal digits without leading zeros. issued_at uses the same form, optionally followed by a decimal point and fractional digits without trailing zeros. The verifier takes the accepted Hub key and interval from the agreed publication settings.
Retrieval. Relative to the agreed topic base URL, GET heartbeat/latest returns the latest heartbeat as one JSON object and GET heartbeat returns the full list as an array. GET heartbeat?from={timestamp}&until={timestamp} returns the heartbeats with from <= issued_at < until, and an omitted bound leaves that end open. If conflicting signed heartbeats arise, the service keeps both.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
CBC and Correction References
Offer and acceptance. The offer is an ordinary entry whose payload names the subject of the agreement, the parties, the conditions and the time of the offer. The acceptance carries subject_hash, the offer’s Event ID, together with its acknowledgement of the terms. The reference binds the acceptance to that exact offer wherever the acceptance sits in the chain. When the parties require the acceptance to follow the offer immediately, its prev_hash also equals the offer’s Event ID. Whether subject_hash becomes an entry member or a payload field remains open, and it belongs to neither the base nor the Mint members above. Either way, the signature must cover it, directly or through the payload hash.

Corrections
A statement that addresses an earlier entry refers to it through subject_hash, exactly as an acceptance does, while prev_hash still names the immediately preceding line. The payload says which kind of statement the entry is and carries its substance. When the accepting party disputes an offer, it withholds acceptance and records a signed objection that refers to the offer, so the CBC stays pending and the objection says why; a resolution is a further signed entry that refers to the objection. Application policy decides how it recognises an author’s replacement credential.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
Key Registries
A registry (What a Signature Proves) is a topic whose entries are binding events and whose keeper accepts each binding. Each is an ordinary entry under the entry specification with no additional member. Four kinds of binding event exist, and the payload says which kind an entry is:

Register. The subject key signs the offer, so the entry’s public_key is the key the binding covers. A person’s passkey cannot sign an entry, so for a person the producing system signs the offer and the person confirms it in a Mint entry (WebAuthn checks), and the binding covers attester_key. The payload carries the subject type (person, device, service or registry root), an identity reference, a role and the hash of the enrolment evidence. The keeper signs the acceptance with subject_hash naming the offer (CBC references). The binding stands from the acceptance’s position; before that it is pending, and a refusal is a signed objection (corrections).
Rotate. The new key signs the offer, whose payload names the binding it replaces by Event ID, and the keeper accepts. A registry’s root key rotates the same way: the new root signs the offer and the current root accepts, and holders follow the new root from that position.
Retire. The keeper signs one entry that names the binding by Event ID. Signatures the key made before that position stand.
Compromise. The keeper signs one entry that names the binding and the time from which the key is suspect, which may precede the entry. The verifier reports each entry the key signed at or after that time and before the claim’s position as inside a claimed compromise window and leaves the decision to the application.

Under the payload rule, the binding payload travels with its salt, so a holder resolves keys offline; the enrolment evidence, including any personal details, stays with the keeper under its access policy. Each topic declares the registries it accepts, by registry topic and root key, directly or through a binding in a registry it already accepts, and a change to that declaration is a CBC that the topic’s other parties countersign. When two accepted registries bind one key differently, the verifier reports conflicting, keeps both bindings and leaves the decision to the application.
Three conventions remain open, each with the constraint an answer must meet:

Declaration encoding. How the first entry carries the accepted registries and the scope of each. Constraint: every holder can read it without the payload access policy, and it meets the open convention that binds a topic to its first entry (entry specification).
Entry-to-binding reference. Whether a verifier resolves a key by lookup in the accepted registries at verification time, as this appendix assumes, or an entry carries a reference to its binding. Constraint: a carried reference needs a new entry revision, because an unknown member makes an entry malformed.
Attribution outcomes. The states the verifier reports for a key, modelled on the heartbeat outcomes: bound, pending, unbound, conflicting, retired before signing and inside a claimed compromise window are the candidates. Constraint: signature validity, binding evidence, compromise status and authorisation stay separate.

The foundation stewards these conventions (Protocol Stewardship). The questions it settles first:

Who may keep a registry that others accept, and what enrolment evidence each must demand.
How a keeper recovers when it loses its root key or a thief rotates the root first: a new first entry, and each accepting topic’s countersigned change to its declaration.
Whether any rule beyond reporting decides between two accepted registries that disagree.
How far back a compromise claim may reach, and who must countersign one.
How long a keeper retains enrolment evidence, and how it deletes it.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
Payload Access and Export
The application attaches the access policy to the payload, never to payload_ref. An authorised holder can export public payloads with their salts, keeping the exact bytes the hash covers and linking each to its payload_ref or Event ID, so others can verify them offline. Salt length and encoding, including the boundary between salt and payload, remain open in the specification. A public key or a payload hash can still be linkable to a person, so neither is automatically anonymous under GDPR.

title: Appendix: Specification
text:
Verifier Outcomes for Heartbeat Evidence
The verifier reports heartbeat evidence as missing when no authenticated heartbeat for the topic is retrievable, stale when the latest one falls outside the application’s freshness window, or conflicting when authenticated heartbeats or the supplied history disagree at a covered position. For that topic, the application pauses the actions that need verified shared evidence, keeps capturing and queuing new events locally, and escalates. A conflict keeps both heartbeats for reconciliation.

title: Appendix: Comparison Tables
text:
Standards Lineage
This appendix holds the comparison tables that 3  Consensus by Comparison relies on and shows how EventChain relates to existing transparency and provenance systems.
EventChain sits in a lineage of cryptographic accountability systems. Haber and Stornetta established hash-linked time-stamping as a way to make document history tamper-evident without a conventional record-keeper (Haber and Stornetta 1991). Certificate Transparency and Trillian turned append-only transparency logs into operational infrastructure for public certificates (Laurie et al. 2013; Google 2026). SCITT generalises transparency receipts for supply-chain statements using COSE/CBOR and external transparency services (Birkholz et al. 2026). KERI focuses on self-certifying identifiers and key-event logs for decentralised identity (Smith 2019). Parakeet demonstrates privacy-preserving transparency through public commitments, private querying, and verifiable proof (Malvai et al. 2023). TrustChain shows that a blockchain can preserve data while leaving truth at origin unresolved (Malik et al. 2019).
EventChain borrows the durable lessons and chooses a different operating point: identity-bound event authorship, portable proof artefacts, role-aware distribution, lightweight verification, and optional public time anchoring.
SCITT and EventChain operate at different layers. SCITT answers whether a transparency service registered a signed statement; its receipt can accompany the statement for verification (Birkholz et al. 2026, sec. 7). EventChain preserves producer-signed entries and their sequence in a portable file. An organisation could register an EventChain head in a SCITT transparency service for additional public auditability.

text:
Choosing an Approach
Table 9 sets EventChain beside the other ways of keeping provenance. The approaches combine: an organisation might keep ERP audit trails internally, use EventChain for the evidence shared across organisations, and register heads in a SCITT service for public accountability.



Table 9: Approaches to provenance: when each fits and where it falls short











Approach
Works well when
Falls short when
Adoption condition




Do nothing
Single-party control, low stakes, short lifecycles, negligible dispute risk
Multiple handoffs, regulatory scrutiny, or long-lived histories where reconstruction costs compound
Risk exposure remains below the cost of any provenance system


ERP audit trails
All relevant parties share one system, or a dominant buyer mandates platform access
Records must survive beyond the platform operator, or partners lack ERP access
Organisational control spans the full lifecycle


Document signing (e-signatures)
Point-in-time attestation between known parties, such as contract execution or inspection sign-off
Continuity matters, because signed documents do not chain into a verifiable sequence across several actors
The proof need is a single moment


Managed compliance portals
Compliance requires a portal with public access and standardised data models
The portal cannot produce independently verifiable evidence, or the history must outlive the platform vendor
A single vendor can credibly serve the history’s full lifetime


VC/DID credentials
Interoperable identity claims across organisations, where selective disclosure and the subject’s control of its credentials matter
The question is the order and integrity of events, which credentials do not carry
Identity portability is the primary requirement


Enterprise distributed ledger
High-value, multi-party transactions that need shared state no single operator controls
Consortium formation stalls, costs exclude smaller participants, or throughput requirements exceed consensus limits
All parties can fund node infrastructure and governance


SCITT transparency registry
Public accountability for signed statements, with receipts that can travel with those statements
Statement storage, discovery, and distribution need an implementation beyond the registry specification
A transparency service exists and holders accept its verification keys and policies


EventChain with an application layer
Identified parties in different organisations need a long-lived history each can verify, including participants who cannot fund ledger infrastructure
Strangers settle payments with one another, or one organisation controls the whole process and nobody outside needs to verify
At least one party needs proof that survives beyond any single platform
